section.title: The Land Yet to Be Conquered
section.sectionRationale: The book turns from conquest to allotment. Joshua is now old, yet much land remains to be possessed, and God commands him to divide the whole land as an inheritance even before it is fully taken, promising, I Myself will drive out the nations. The chapter then records the inheritance Moses had already given the eastern tribes, and the striking note that Levi's inheritance is the LORD Himself. It is one movement, the command to apportion the land by faith, holding together God's finished promise and its ongoing fulfillment.
section.thesis: Though Joshua is old and much land is still unconquered, God tells him to divide it all by lot as an inheritance, because the giving of the land rests on God's promise, not on what has yet been achieved; and in the middle of the land grants stands a deeper truth, that for the tribe of Levi the LORD Himself is the inheritance.
section.frameNote: Three beats: the command to divide the land that remains, verses 1 to 7; the eastern inheritance Moses gave and Levi's portion in the LORD, verses 8 to 14; and the detailed allotments of Reuben, Gad, and eastern Manasseh, verses 15 to 33.

units.label: The command to divide the land that remains
units.note: I Myself will drive them out; divide it as an inheritance

verses.text: Now Joshua was old and well along in years, and the LORD said to him, “You are old and well along in years, but very much of the land remains to be possessed.
This is the land that remains: All the territory of the Philistines and the Geshurites,

from the Shihor east of Egypt to the territory of Ekron on the north (considered to be Canaanite territory), that of the five Philistine rulers of Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron, as well as that of the Avvites;
to the south, all the land of the Canaanites, from Mearah of the Sidonians to Aphek, as far as the border of the Amorites;
the land of the Gebalites; and all Lebanon to the east, from Baal-gad below Mount Hermon to Lebo-hamath.

All the inhabitants of the hill country from Lebanon to Misrephoth-maim, all the Sidonians, I Myself will {{yarash|drive out}} before the Israelites. Be sure to divide it by {{goral|lot}} as an inheritance to Israel, as I have commanded you.
Now therefore divide this land as an {{nachalah|inheritance}} to the nine tribes and the half-tribe of Manasseh.”

units.label: The eastern inheritance and Levi's portion in the LORD

verses.text: The other half of Manasseh, along with the Reubenites and Gadites, had received the inheritance Moses had given them beyond the Jordan to the east, just as Moses the servant of the LORD had assigned to them:
The area from Aroer on the rim of the Arnon Valley, along with the city in the middle of the valley, the whole plateau of Medeba as far as Dibon,
and all the cities of Sihon king of the Amorites who reigned in Heshbon, as far as the border of the Ammonites;
also Gilead and the territory of the Geshurites and Maacathites, all of Mount Hermon, and all Bashan as far as Salecah,
the whole kingdom of Og in Bashan, who had reigned in Ashtaroth and Edrei and had remained as a remnant of the Rephaim. Moses had struck them down and dispossessed them,
but the Israelites did not drive out the Geshurites or the Maacathites. So Geshur and Maacath dwell among the Israelites to this day.
To the tribe of Levi, however, Moses had given no inheritance. The food offerings to the LORD, the God of Israel, are their inheritance, just as He had promised them.

units.label: The allotments of Reuben, Gad, and eastern Manasseh
units.note: the portions Moses gave on the plains of Moab

verses.text: This is what Moses had given to the clans of the tribe of Reuben:
The territory from Aroer on the rim of the Arnon Valley, along with the city in the middle of the valley, to the whole plateau beyond Medeba,
to Heshbon and all its cities on the plateau, including Dibon, Bamoth-baal, Beth-baal-meon,
Jahaz, Kedemoth, Mephaath,
Kiriathaim, Sibmah, Zereth-shahar on the hill in the valley,
Beth-peor, the slopes of Pisgah, and Beth-jeshimoth,

all the cities of the plateau and all the kingdom of Sihon king of the Amorites, who reigned in Heshbon until Moses killed him and the chiefs of Midian (Evi, Rekem, Zur, Hur, and Reba), the princes of Sihon who lived in the land.
The Israelites also killed the diviner Balaam son of Beor along with the others they put to the sword.
And the border of the Reubenites was the bank of the Jordan. This was the inheritance of the clans of the Reubenites, including the cities and villages.
This is what Moses had given to the clans of the tribe of Gad:
The territory of Jazer, all the cities of Gilead, and half the land of the Ammonites as far as Aroer, near Rabbah;
the territory from Heshbon to Ramath-mizpeh and Betonim, and from Mahanaim to the border of Debir;

and in the valley, Beth-haram, Beth-nimrah, Succoth, and Zaphon, with the rest of the kingdom of Sihon king of Heshbon (the territory on the east side of the Jordan up to the edge of the Sea of Chinnereth).
This was the inheritance of the clans of the Gadites, including the cities and villages.
This is what Moses had given to the clans of the half-tribe of Manasseh, that is, to half the tribe of the descendants of Manasseh:
The territory from Mahanaim through all Bashan, all the kingdom of Og king of Bashan, including all the towns of Jair that are in Bashan, sixty cities;
half of Gilead; and Ashtaroth and Edrei, the royal cities of Og in Bashan. All this was for the clans of the descendants of Machir son of Manasseh, that is, half of the descendants of Machir.
These were the portions Moses had given them on the plains of Moab beyond the Jordan, east of Jericho.
To the tribe of Levi, however, Moses had given no inheritance. The LORD, the God of Israel, is their inheritance, just as He had promised them.

yarash.gloss: To take possession of, dispossess, drive out. God promises, I Myself will drive out the remaining nations, using the key conquest verb but now with God as the emphatic subject. The land still to be possessed will be taken not by Israel's exhausted, aging strength but by the LORD Himself, so the tribes may divide it in faith while the driving out continues.

goral.gloss: A lot, the casting of lots to determine God's decision. The land is divided by goral, so that each tribe's portion is seen as assigned by the LORD, not won by favoritism or human bargaining, Proverbs 16:33. The lot removes human striving from the allotment and grounds each inheritance in God's own choice.

nachalah.gloss: Inheritance, allotted possession, heritage. The land is Israel's nachalah, divided among the tribes as a gift by promise. Yet the chapter's deepest note is that Levi's nachalah is not land at all: the LORD Himself, and the offerings made to Him, are their inheritance, a truth that points to the highest good of all God's people, to have God as their portion.

basic.context: The conquest is largely done, and Joshua is now an old man, but God points out that much land still remains to be taken, and He commands Joshua to divide the whole land among the tribes as an inheritance, even the parts not yet possessed. The reason is a promise: I Myself will drive them out before you. The tribes are to receive their portions by faith, trusting God to complete what He has begun. The chapter then records the land Moses had already given the eastern tribes, Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh, in detail. Twice it pauses to say something remarkable about the tribe of Levi: they get no land, because the LORD Himself is their inheritance. The question underneath is: how do God's people live between a promise given and a promise not yet fully realized, and what is the greatest inheritance of all?
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative that shifts the book from conquest to allotment. The detailed geography is not directly applicable to us, but the chapter carries rich theology: God gives the inheritance as a promise to be received by faith even before it is fully seen, and the LORD Himself is the true inheritance of His people. The note that Israel did not drive out some peoples also honestly flags the incomplete obedience that will trouble later chapters.
basic.originalLanguages: God says He will Himself yarash, drive out, the nations that remain. The land is divided by goral, by lot, as God's own assignment. It is Israel's nachalah, inheritance; yet Levi's nachalah is the LORD Himself.
basic.typology: The already and not yet of the land, given by promise but not fully possessed, pictures the Christian's inheritance in Christ, secured and yet awaited. And Levi having the LORD as their inheritance foreshadows the deepest truth of the gospel, that God Himself is the portion of His people, fulfilled in Christ.
basic.christ: Levi's portion, the LORD Himself, points to the greatest gift of the gospel: not merely things from God but God Himself, given to us in Christ. As the psalmist says, the LORD is my portion; so in Christ we receive God as our inheritance and are made His. The land held by promise yet still being possessed mirrors our inheritance, guaranteed in Christ and awaiting full possession.
basic.god: God is the faithful promise-keeper who commands His people to act on His word before it is fully fulfilled, pledging, I Myself will drive them out. He is the God who assigns each portion by lot, sovereign over the inheritance. And He is Himself the highest inheritance, the portion of His people, greater than any land.
basic.crossReferences: Numbers 18 explains that the LORD is the Levites' portion. Psalm 16 rejoices that the LORD is my chosen portion and inheritance. Deuteronomy 3 records the eastern allotment under Moses. And Ephesians 1 speaks of the inheritance guaranteed to believers in Christ by the Spirit.
basic.oneStory: As the land is divided, God commands His people to receive the inheritance by faith while He completes the driving out, and He reveals that for Levi the LORD Himself is the inheritance. This points to the gospel: an inheritance secured in Christ yet awaited, and the greatest gift of all, God Himself as the portion of His people.

context.literary:
Chapter 13 begins the second major division of the book, the allotment section running through chapter 21, with a formal marker Hebrew narrative reserves for hinge points: God speaking directly to Joshua, something recorded only a few times across the whole book, compare 1:1 and 5:13-15. The direct address itself signals that a new phase, not merely a new topic, is beginning.

Structurally, the chapter is built as a careful frame. It opens with God's own command to divide land not yet possessed, verses 1 to 7, moves into the record of what Moses had already granted east of the Jordan, verses 8 to 13, and closes that unit with a statement about Levi's portion in verse 14. The following block, verses 15 to 32, itemizes, tribe by tribe, the specific boundaries and cities Moses assigned to Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh, only to close the whole chapter, verse 33, with the identical Levi statement repeated almost word for word.

This repetition, an inclusio in Hebrew narrative, functions like a pair of bookends: whatever sits between two nearly identical statements is meant to be read in their light, so that the entire detailed land grant to the eastern tribes is deliberately framed by, and thereby subordinated to, the truth that Levi's portion is the LORD Himself. The chapter's structure is quietly making an argument before a single boundary line is drawn: land is a real gift, but it is not the greatest one.
context.historical:
The land still unconquered in this chapter was real, named territory, not a vague frontier. The five Philistine city-states, Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron, verses 2 to 3, formed a coastal confederation whose rulers Scripture consistently calls by a distinct term rather than the ordinary Hebrew word for king used throughout Joshua 12, a signal that these southern coastal powers, likely recent arrivals from the Aegean world in this period, organized themselves differently from the inland Canaanite city-kingdoms Israel had already defeated.

To the north lay Geshur and the Sidonian coastline, Phoenician territory Israel would never subdue by conquest; verse 13 admits plainly that Geshur and Maacath simply remained, unconquered, among the Israelites to this day, the book's own footnote on the limits of the settlement it describes. Judges later explains theologically what this chapter only records historically: the LORD Himself left certain nations, including these same Philistine rulers, to test Israel's obedience and to train generations too young to have known war, Judges 3:1-4.

The territorial promise was not abandoned, only deferred. Centuries later, under Solomon, Israel's influence would in fact reach from the Euphrates to the border of Egypt and the very land of the Philistines, tribute flowing in from kingdoms Joshua's generation never touched, 1 Kings 4:21,24, a slow-motion answer to the LORD's ancient pledge in this chapter, I Myself will drive them out.
context.canonical:
The declaration that Levi has no portion but the LORD Himself did not originate here; Numbers 18:20, Deuteronomy 10:9, 12:12, and 18:1-2 all establish it well before Israel crosses the Jordan, so Joshua 13 is citing settled covenant law rather than introducing new theology, as if to make sure the point survives into the record of the actual land division. The same formula recurs once more, almost verbatim, at Joshua 18:7, when the allotment resumes after the tabernacle is set up at Shiloh, showing how central this refrain was to how Israel understood its priestly tribe.

Centuries later, when the writer of Hebrews wants to explain why the priesthood needed to change, from Levi to an order after Melchizedek, part of the argument is precisely that Levi's portion was never landed wealth but service and dependence on God, Hebrews 7:11-12, a dependence the New Testament extends to the whole believing community, called a royal priesthood belonging to God alone, 1 Peter 2:9.

The chapter's other major theme, land promised but not yet possessed, becomes explicit devotional theology only later, in Hebrews 11's portrait of the patriarchs who died without receiving what was promised yet welcomed it from a distance, and in Paul's confident claim that every one of God's promises is Yes in Christ, however long the interval between the promise and its full delivery, 2 Corinthians 1:20.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The chapter means to hold two things together that could easily pull apart: God's astonishing confidence in His own promise, dividing land Israel had not yet set foot on, and total honesty about what remained undone, naming the Philistines, the Geshurites, and the Sidonians by name rather than glossing over the gap between promise and possession.

The author also clearly intends readers to notice, twice, in nearly identical language, that Levi's portion in this whole scheme is different in kind from every other tribe's, not a share of ground but the LORD Himself and the offerings made to Him. Placed at the very start of the allotment section, this double statement functions as an interpretive key for everything that follows: every tribal boundary the reader is about to wade through for eight chapters should be read against the backdrop of a tribe that received something greater than any of them, a reminder that the land itself was always meant to point beyond itself.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The specific boundary markers of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh describe a one-time historical settlement and prescribe nothing for later readers to imitate geographically. What is transferable is the pattern the chapter models: receiving God's promises in confident advance of full possession, naming plainly what remains unresolved rather than pretending otherwise, and recognizing that some of God's people are given no land inheritance at all, only Himself, without treating that as deprivation.

Applied today, the chapter cautions against two opposite errors, presuming the whole promise is already fully realized when Scripture itself admits land yet to be possessed, and despairing that a promise partly fulfilled is not really being kept, when in fact its slow unfolding, as with the eastern tribes' inheritance already decades old by this point, is itself part of how God fulfills His word.

debates.question: Why command the land divided when so much was still unconquered?

views.label: Because the inheritance rests on God's promise, not on completed conquest
views.case: God says I Myself will drive them out; the tribes are to receive their portions in faith, trusting God to finish what He began, so the allotment is an act of confidence in the promise, teaching that God's people lay hold of His gifts by faith before they see them fully realized, Hebrews 11:1.

views.label: To set a mandate that would summon ongoing faith and obedience
views.case: By assigning land not yet taken, God gives each tribe both a gift and a task, a portion to possess as they continue to trust and obey; the arrangement guards against complacency, since the later failure to drive out the nations, already hinted at in verse 13, will show what happens when faith and obedience falter.

debates.bearing: Both readings hold the already and not yet together: the inheritance is truly given by promise, yet it must be entered by faith, a pattern that shapes the Christian life lived between Christ's finished work and its full consummation.

debates.question: Does verse 13's admission, that Geshur and Maacath were not driven out, describe simple military failure or something else?

views.label: A failure of faith and follow-through
views.case: The verb built through Joshua 12 for total dispossession is the same verb God uses of Himself in 13:6, so when verse 13 says Israel did not drive out these peoples, it is measuring Israel's obedience against God's own stated intention, and the honest admission anticipates the far larger catalogue of failures Judges 1 will record.

views.label: A limited exception within an otherwise faithful record
views.case: Only two named peoples are excepted here, against dozens of successful conquests recorded in chapters 6 to 12, so the note functions less as an indictment of Israel's generation and more as a specific, minor gap, one small unresolved detail inside a chapter mainly occupied with celebrating a completed inheritance for the eastern tribes.

debates.bearing: Both readings can stand together: the exception is narrow enough not to overturn the record of chapters 1 to 12, yet Scripture never lets even a narrow failure pass unmentioned, training readers to notice compromise early rather than only once it has multiplied, as it does by the time of Judges.

study.originalLanguages:
Four features of the underlying Hebrew repay closer attention here. First, the emphatic word I Myself in verse 6 is not something the ordinary form of the verb requires. Hebrew verbs already encode their subject, so adding a separate, independent pronoun for emphasis, as the underlying text does before the verb drive out, is the language's way of underlining the subject: not Joshua, not Israel's army, but the LORD Himself will finish what remains. The emphasis matters because Joshua by this point is old, and the grammar itself removes the burden of finishing the conquest from his aging shoulders and places it squarely on God.

Second, the chapter's land grants are described with two different, carefully chosen verbs. What Moses did for the eastern tribes is repeatedly natan, to give, a plain verb of gift used again and again, verses 8, 15, 24, and 29, while what Israel must still do to the remaining nations is yarash, to dispossess or take possession, the conquest verb already familiar from chapter 12. The land is given as pure gift; it becomes actually possessed only through being entered and taken. Grace and effort are not confused in the vocabulary: the tribes never earn what Moses already gave them, yet they must still walk into what the LORD still promises to clear.

Third, the double statement about Levi pairs two near-synonyms Deuteronomy uses together elsewhere, a portion and an inheritance, neither of which Levi receives among the tribes. Piling up two words for possession only to deny both to Levi is a deliberate rhetorical stress: it is not merely that Levi's land allotment is smaller or different, but that in the very categories used to measure every other tribe's share, Levi has nothing, because something greater stands in its place.

Fourth, the land is divided by goral, lot, a term whose associated imagery elsewhere describes the lot falling, as though the decision drops out of human hands entirely. Proverbs reflects on exactly this mechanism: the lot is cast into the lap, but every decision from it is the LORD's, Proverbs 16:33. Reading goral against that verse turns what looks like chance into its opposite, a deliberately impersonal method chosen because it removes any tribe's ability to claim favoritism, leaving the assignment entirely in God's hand even while human beings cast the actual lot.

typology.type: Land given by promise, entered only by ongoing faith
typology.fulfillment: The tribes receive their boundaries on paper before the last enemy is cleared from them, a pattern Hebrews applies to every believer under the new covenant: all these people died in faith without having received the things promised, yet they welcomed them from a distance and openly acknowledged that they were strangers on the earth, seeking a better, heavenly country, Hebrews 11:13-16. The correspondence sharpens in Christ, whose resurrection guarantees an inheritance kept in heaven rather than merely deferred on earth, 1 Peter 1:4; the type falls short in that Israel's remaining land could still be lost to unfaithfulness, while the believer's inheritance, sealed by the Spirit, cannot be forfeited, Ephesians 1:13-14.

typology.type: The LORD Himself as Levi's inheritance
typology.fulfillment: No other tribe receives this kind of portion, only Levi, so that the priestly tribe's identity is defined entirely by nearness to God rather than by property. Believers in Christ inherit exactly this, not merely gifts but God as their portion, echoed in the psalmist's confession that God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever, Psalm 73:26, and in Paul's description of every believer, not only a priestly class, as an heir of God and co-heir with Christ, Romans 8:17. The type escalates here: what was true of one tribe under the old covenant becomes true of every believer under the new.

typology.type: God's pledge, I Myself will drive them out
typology.fulfillment: The promise rests on divine initiative rather than Israel's remaining strength, matching Paul's confidence that He who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion, Philippians 1:6, and his sweeping claim that every promise of God finds its Yes in Christ, however long deferred, 2 Corinthians 1:20. Where Joshua 13 still leaves named enemies unconquered at the time of writing, the New Testament's confidence rests on a finished work, the cross and resurrection already accomplished, so that what remains is the certain outworking of a victory already won rather than one still being decided.

study.christ:
This chapter opens with an old man being told that the work is not finished, and closes with a tribe whose only portion is God Himself; both notes find their full answer in Christ. Joshua, however faithful, grows old and cannot complete the conquest by his own strength; Scripture elsewhere is careful to distinguish him from the one he only foreshadows, since if Joshua had given Israel final rest, God would not have spoken later of another day of rest still to come, Hebrews 4:8-9. The gap this chapter admits, real land still needing to be taken, is not incidental; it is the gap every merely human deliverer eventually reveals, and it is precisely the gap Christ was sent to close permanently.

Christ answers the promise, I Myself will drive them out, verse 6, with an equally emphatic pledge of His own, that He will build His church and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it, Matthew 16:18. Where Joshua depended on an aging body and a partially obedient nation to finish God's work, Christ finishes what He begins without needing a successor; there is no thirteenth chapter in the gospel that must admit unconquered territory still remaining after Him.

The chapter's other pole, that the LORD is Levi's whole inheritance, points to Christ even more directly, because in Him that priestly nearness to God is no longer the special possession of one tribe. Hebrews shows that Christ holds His priesthood permanently, because He continues forever, and is therefore able to save completely those who come to God through Him, Hebrews 7:24-25; He does not pass the office to a successor the way Aaron's sons had to, because His life, and His priesthood, never ends. What made Levi different from every other tribe, having God rather than ground as an inheritance, becomes in Christ the shared inheritance of everyone who comes to God through Him, priest and non-priest alike, so that the whole church is now what Levi alone once was, a people whose true portion is the LORD Himself.
study.god:
This chapter reveals a God unhurried by human limitation. Joshua is old, the conquest incomplete, yet the LORD does not treat Joshua's age as a crisis to be managed; He simply states the plain truth, very much land remains, and takes personal responsibility for finishing it, I Myself will drive them out. God's timetable is never hostage to the strength of the leader currently serving Him; when one servant's strength fails, His own does not.

He is also, in the same body of law that first explains this chapter's Levi statement, revealed as scrupulously impartial. Deuteronomy explains why Levi has no inheritance among the tribes, the LORD is his inheritance, in the very passage that describes God as one who shows no partiality and accepts no bribe, Deuteronomy 10:9,17. The God who assigns each tribe's ground by lot rather than by human negotiation is the same God who cannot be bought or favored; the impartial method of allotment, verse 6, and the impartial character behind it are one and the same.

He is a God who gives identity as well as property. Every other tribe is defined in this chapter by a boundary line; Levi alone is defined by a relationship, the LORD Himself. That this distinction is stated twice, almost verbatim, verses 14 and 33, shows a God who does not merely tolerate variety among His people's callings but deliberately builds it into the structure of the nation, so that some serve Him through farming and border disputes and others through unmediated nearness to His altar, and neither vocation is treated as lesser.

Finally, He is candid rather than image-conscious. A God concerned only with appearing triumphant would not have allowed verse 13's plain admission that Geshur and Maacath were never driven out to stand inside His own book. That He does allow it says something important about His character: He is not threatened by an honest record of incomplete obedience, because His faithfulness does not depend on His people's performance being flawless.

crossReferences.note: Long before Israel reaches the plains of Moab, God already tells Aaron directly that he will have no inheritance in the land, for I am your portion and your inheritance among the Israelites. Joshua 13 is not introducing a new arrangement for the priestly tribe but recording the fulfillment, decades later, of a settled promise.

Moses recalls that the LORD set Levi apart to carry the ark and stand before Him precisely because he would have no portion or inheritance among his brothers. The same chapter calls God one who shows no partiality, tying Levi's unique calling to the character of the God who assigns it.

The law states plainly that the Levitical priests will eat the fire offerings as their inheritance, since the LORD Himself is their inheritance, as He promised them. Joshua 13:14 repeats this almost word for word, showing how carefully the conquest generation preserved Moses' own language.

When the allotment resumes at Shiloh, the narrator repeats the Levi formula a third time, adding that Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh have already received their inheritance beyond the Jordan. The repetition across three chapters shows how central this refrain was to Israel's memory of the land division.

The nations still standing at the end of Joshua 13, the five Philistine rulers among them, are named again here as the very peoples the LORD deliberately left, to test Israel's obedience and train generations too young to have fought. What chapter 13 leaves as an open question, Judges answers with a purpose.

Centuries after Joshua's death, Solomon's kingdom reaches from the Euphrates to the border of Egypt, including tribute from the very Philistine territory Joshua 13 lists as still unconquered. The promise deferred in Joshua's day is not abandoned; it is fulfilled on a longer timeline than any single generation could see.

The patriarchs, and by extension every generation that received land or promise only in part, died without having received the things they were promised, yet welcomed them from a distance and sought a better, heavenly country. Joshua 13's unfinished land grant is one early chapter in that same long story of promise held by faith.

Paul tells believers that if they are children of God, they are heirs, heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ. What Levi alone possessed under the old covenant, the LORD as inheritance rather than land, becomes in Christ the shared inheritance of every believer, not a priestly class alone.

The Holy Spirit is described as the guarantee of the believer's inheritance until final redemption. The tribes of Joshua 13 hold their eastern land as an already-settled fact while the western allotment still awaits completion; the Spirit performs a similar double role for believers, sealing what is certain while what is promised is still being fully possessed.

study.oneStory:
From the beginning, inheritance has been how God relates to His people: Adam was given a garden to keep, Israel is given a land to possess, and in both cases the ground was never the point so much as the relationship the ground made possible. Joshua 13 sits at a strange, honest juncture in that larger story, a chapter where the gift is pronounced complete in principle, divide the land, verse 7, while remaining incomplete in fact, very much land remains, verse 1. That tension between what God has declared and what is not yet fully seen runs through the whole of redemptive history, from Abraham who died in a land he did not yet own outright, Hebrews 11:13, to a church that already possesses every spiritual blessing in Christ while still waiting for a resurrection body and a renewed earth, Ephesians 1:3 and Romans 8:23.

Inside that larger tension, the chapter drops one line that quietly reorients everything: Levi has no land, because the LORD is his inheritance. It is a small, easily missed anticipation of what the whole story is ultimately building toward, not more territory but God Himself given to His people without remainder. The tabernacle at the center of Israel's camp, the temple later built in Jerusalem, and finally the incarnation, God tabernacling among us in flesh, John 1:14, are successive answers to the same longing this verse names, that the deepest inheritance a person can receive is not a plot of ground but the presence of God.

The story does not end with unfinished conquest. It ends, in Revelation's last vision, with no more temple in the city, because the Lord God and the Lamb are its temple, and God's own people will see His face, Revelation 21:22 and 22:4. Joshua 13's aging leader and unconquered borders give way, in the end, to a King who never grows old and a land that needs no further conquest, because every enemy is finally gone.

quiz.q: What did God tell the aging Joshua about the land?

options.text: That much land still remained to be possessed, and it should be divided as an inheritance even so.
options.note: Verses 1 to 7 record God's command to divide the land, though much was unconquered.

options.text: That the conquest was entirely finished and nothing remained.
options.note: The opposite: God stressed that very much of the land remained to be possessed.

options.text: That Israel had failed and would lose the land.
options.note: God was not pronouncing failure; He promised to drive out the nations and commanded the land divided.

options.text: That Joshua must conquer it all himself before dividing it.
options.note: God said He Himself would drive out the nations and told Joshua to divide the land now, by faith.

quiz.q: How was the land to be divided among the tribes?

options.text: By lot, so that each portion was received as the LORD's own assignment.
options.note: Verse 6 commands division by lot, grounding each inheritance in God's choice.

options.text: By auction to the highest bidder.
options.note: There was no auction; the land was assigned by lot as God's gift, not sold.

options.text: By letting each tribe seize whatever it could take.
options.note: The allotment was orderly and by lot, not a free-for-all seizure.

options.text: By Joshua's personal preference for each tribe.
options.note: It was decided by lot as God's assignment, not by Joshua's favoritism.

quiz.q: What was the inheritance of the tribe of Levi?

options.text: The LORD Himself, and the offerings made to Him; they received no land.
options.note: Verses 14 and 33 state twice that the LORD is Levi's inheritance.

options.text: The largest and best portion of land.
options.note: Levi received no land portion at all; their inheritance was the LORD Himself.

options.text: A share of every other tribe's harvest, but a small plot of land too.
options.note: They lived among cities with pasturelands, but the text stresses they had no land inheritance; the LORD was their portion.

options.text: Nothing at all, not even God's provision.
options.note: They had the greatest inheritance of all, the LORD Himself, and His offerings for provision.

quiz.q: Why did God command the land divided before it was fully conquered?

options.text: Because the inheritance rests on God's promise to drive out the nations, received by faith.
options.note: God's pledge, I Myself will drive them out, grounds the allotment in faith, not in completed conquest.

options.text: Because God had given up on conquering the rest.
options.note: God had not given up; He promised to complete the driving out Himself.

options.text: Because the tribes demanded their land immediately.
options.note: The command came from God, resting on His promise, not from the tribes' demands.

options.text: Because the remaining land did not matter.
options.note: The land mattered and was included in the inheritance; God promised to secure it.

quiz.q: How does Levi's inheritance point to the gospel?

options.text: Having the LORD Himself as their portion pictures the gift of God Himself to His people in Christ.
options.note: The LORD as Levi's inheritance foreshadows God given as our portion in Christ, Psalm 16:5, Romans 8:17.

options.text: It shows that God's people should expect no blessings at all.
options.note: Levi lacked land, but had the greatest blessing, God Himself; the point is not the absence of blessing.

options.text: It teaches that only priests can truly know God.
options.note: In Christ all believers have God as their portion, not only a priestly class.

options.text: It has no connection to the gospel.
options.note: The LORD as inheritance is one of the richest gospel pointers, fulfilled in God giving Himself to us in Christ.

questions: God told the tribes to receive land by faith before it was fully theirs. Where is God calling you to lay hold of one of His promises by faith before you can see it fully realized?
The land was assigned by lot, as God's own choosing. How does trusting that your circumstances are assigned by a sovereign, loving God change the way you view your lot in life?
Levi's inheritance was the LORD Himself. Is God Himself your treasure, or are you mainly seeking the gifts He gives rather than God?
Some peoples were not driven out, a hint of incomplete obedience that would cause later trouble. Where might partial obedience in your life be leaving trouble to grow?
In Christ, God gives His people not just blessings but Himself. How would your prayer and worship change if you truly prized having God as your portion above all else?

translationNotes.note: Balaam son of Beor, the diviner who tried to curse Israel in Numbers 22 to 24, was killed in the war against Midian, Numbers 31:8; the note underscores the failure of his hire to curse God's people.

The food offerings to the LORD are the Levites' inheritance in verse 14, while verse 33 says the LORD Himself is their inheritance; the two express one truth, that God and His service are Levi's portion in place of land.
